title: Marta Weinstock-Rosin developed Exelon, a drug for Alzheimer's patients, at the Hebrew University

trailer.text: Prof. Marta Weinstock-Rosin, of the Hebrew University School of Pharmacy, is best known for developing the drug Exelon.
She was born in Vienna, and after her father was arrested for being Jewish, the family fled to England in 1939, where they escaped the Nazis.
In 1969 she immigrated to Israel with her family.
In the 1980s her mother-in-law fell ill with Alzheimer's, and she felt helpless in the face of the lack of medical treatment for the disease.

In 1986 one of the compounds she prepared with Prof. Michael Horev and Dr. Ze'ev Ta-Shema showed activity suitable for treating Alzheimer's. From it came the drug, which was approved in the US in 2000 and for which she won the Israel Prize in 2014.

paragraphs.text: Marta Weinstock-Rosin was born in Vienna in 1935.
After her father was arrested for being Jewish, the family decided to flee to England.
In 1939 they escaped from the Nazis to Britain.
According to the Times of Israel, she is a religious, Orthodox woman.
She studied pharmacy and pharmacology at the University of London.
In her doctoral work, in 1961, she showed the existence of morphine receptors in the body.
In 1969 she was offered a senior position at the University of London.
She preferred to immigrate to Israel with her husband and their three children.
In 1981 she became a professor at the Hebrew University.
In 1983 she was head of a unit at the university, and the sources differ on which one.

stations.title: Her mother-in-law fell ill, and the lab began to work

paragraphs.text: In the 1980s her mother-in-law fell ill with Alzheimer's.
There was no medical treatment for the disease at the time, and she felt helpless.
She persuaded the Director General of the Ministry of Science to let her use research funds she had received from the ministry for this purpose.

In 2003, on receiving the $100,000 prize of the Institute for the Study of Aging in New York (ISOA), she said that it is very difficult to obtain research grants for drug development, and especially in this field.
She headed a team of researchers at the Hebrew University.
In 1986 one of the cholinesterase inhibitors she prepared together with Prof. Michael Horev and Dr. Ze'ev Ta-Shema showed activity suitable for treating Alzheimer's.
From this came the drug rivastigmine, whose trade name is Exelon.
Rivastigmine inhibits the breakdown of acetylcholine by the enzyme acetylcholinesterase.
According to the FDA, the precise mechanism is unknown, and it is thought to work by enhancing cholinergic activity.

stations.title: From the lab to the pharmacies

paragraphs.text: According to Hayadan, it was sold to the Swiss company Sandoz.
According to Hayadan, Sandoz swore Weinstock-Rosin to secrecy about the drug's origin in Israel.
According to Hayadan (2014), the Yissum company sold the drug to the Swiss Sandoz company, and today Novartis markets it under the name Exelon.
In April 2000 Novartis received FDA approval to market Exelon in the US.
It was the third Alzheimer's drug on the American market, after Aricept and Cognex.
It was due to reach the market in May, at a wholesale price of $130 per month.
Novartis also incorporated the compound into the Exelon Patch.
According to the Times of Israel, Novartis incorporated rivastigmine into the Exelon Patch, the first and only skin patch approved by the FDA for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.
Exelon is intended for the treatment of mild to moderate dementia of the Alzheimer's type.
It was administered to more than 5,297 people in clinical trials worldwide.
According to the Jerusalem Post, it has been shown to be effective in treating the symptoms of mild to moderate Alzheimer's, but it does not cure the disease.
The sources disagree on whether it can stop the progress of the disease.

According to Channel 7, the 2003 prize of the Institute for the Study of Aging in New York (ISOA), named for Ann and Harald Gottlieb, was then awarded for the first time, and it was intended for a scientist whose research had a real impact on the development of drugs for Alzheimer's.
According to Arutz 7, in 2002 she was the first woman elected president of the Israel Society for Neuroscience.
In February 2014 Minister of Education Shai Piron announced that she had won the Israel Prize for medical research.
The prize committee's reasoning stated that Exelon improves the quality of life of hundreds of thousands of Alzheimer's patients.
She was due to receive the prize on Independence Day.
A year after receiving the prize, she was also chosen to light one of the 12 torches at the ceremony opening Independence Day.
According to the Times of Israel, Exelon is one of the most important drugs to have emerged from Israeli medical research labs in recent years.
According to the Times of Israel, her research focuses on ladostigil, originally developed with Prof. Moussa Youdim of the Technion and with Teva.
She discovered that at a much lower dose it prevents the deterioration of memory in aging rats, by a different mechanism.
According to Hayadan, she realized that the compound intended for treating Alzheimer's has no advantage over existing cholinesterase inhibitors such as Exelon, as a clinical trial in Europe showed.
A trial of ladostigil in 200 subjects at the stage of mild cognitive impairment was designed to test whether it is possible to prevent the development of Alzheimer's.
The trial was partially funded by the rewards from Exelon.
In 2014 ladostigil was in Phase II clinical trials in Israel and Europe.
She said that people must now be helped to live better-quality lives, by slowing or preventing mental decline.
According to her, proper research requires time and commitment that are sometimes lacking at drug companies, and at universities money is lacking.
Her husband, Prof. Arnold Rosin, is a gerontologist.
He is one of the founders of Melabev, the organization that helps dementia patients and their families.
The couple have four children and 20 grandchildren.
She mentored 59 students.
According to Hayadan, many of them reached senior positions in academia and the pharmaceutical industry.

stations.title: What the drug does not do

paragraphs.text: According to the FDA label, the common side effects of Exelon include nausea, vomiting, anorexia, dyspepsia and asthenia.
In controlled trials, 47% of patients at the therapeutic dose developed nausea, compared with 12% of those who received placebo.
According to the label, there is no evidence that rivastigmine alters the course of the underlying dementing process.
According to the Jerusalem Post, the drug does not cure Alzheimer's.

disagreements.question: Can Exelon stop Alzheimer's, or does it only treat the symptoms?

Jerusalem Post (2014): the drug is effective in treating the symptoms, but does not cure
FDA label: there is no evidence that it alters the course of the dementing process
Times of Israel: head of the Pharmacology department at the Hebrew University
Jerusalem Post: head of the School of Pharmacy

claims.text: לפי תווית ה-FDA, בניסויים מבוקרים 47% מהמטופלים במינון הטיפולי פיתחו בחילה, לעומת 12% בפלצבו.
claims.quote: 47% of the patients treated with an EXELON dose in the therapeutic range of 6 mg to 12 mg per day (n=1189) developed nausea (compared with 12% in placebo).

claims.text: הניסוי מומן בחלקו מתגמולי אקסלון.
claims.quote: and is partially funded by the rewards from Exelon
